Seven Days on the Coastal Trail

By Mara Ellison · Photos by Theo Park · Updated June 4

The trail starts where the road gives up. A gravel lot, a wooden sign, and then nothing but cliffs, wind and a thin line of dirt that follows the coast north for ninety-four miles. We had seven days, two stoves and a plan that we changed every morning.

Most people walk the route from south to north, so that the wind is at their back. We did the same. The first day is easy: long, flat stretches above small beaches, with the ocean on the left and fields of yellow gorse on the right. By the afternoon, our legs had found a rhythm.

Day two: the long climb

The second day is the one that people talk about. The path leaves the beaches and climbs through a forest of old spruce to a ridge that is almost two thousand feet above the water. On a clear day, you can see the next three headlands. On our day, we could see the fog.

“The fog lifted for ten minutes, and in that time we understood why people come back.”

We camped that night in a small clearing near a creek. The water was cold and clear, and the filter worked hard. Dinner was lentils, rice and too much hot sauce. Nobody complained.

Left: the beach below Gull Point at low tide. Right: sunset on day four, and the harbor at Port Ansel.

The last morning

On the seventh day, the trail comes down from the cliffs into a small harbor town. There is a bakery next to the bus stop. We were there when it opened, and we stayed until the bus came. It was the best bread any of us had ever eaten, which is what seven days of lentils will do.
